title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 5
q: Suppose $f \colon X \to Y$ is continuous for metric spaces $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$. Show that if $X$ is connected, then $f(X)$ is connected.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 7
q: A continuous $f \colon X \to Y$ between metric spaces $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ is said to be proper if for every compact set $K \subset Y$, the set $f^{-1}(K)$ is compact. Suppose a continuous $f \colon (0,1) \to (0,1)$ is proper and $\{ x_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a sequence in $(0,1)$ converging to $0$. Show that $\bigl\{ f(x_n) \bigr\}_{n=1}^\infty$ has no subsequence that converges in $(0,1)$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 8
q: Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces and $f \colon X \to Y$ be a one-to-one and onto continuous function. Suppose $X$ is compact. Prove that the inverse $f^{-1} \colon Y \to X$ is continuous.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 9
q:
Take the metric space of continuous functions $C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$. Let $k \colon [0,1] \times [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be a continuous function. Given $f \in C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$ define

$$\varphi_f(x) := \int_0^1 k(x,y) f(y) \,dy .$$

(a) Show that $T(f) := \varphi_f$ defines a function $T \colon C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr) \to C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$.

(b) Show that $T$ is continuous.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 11
q:
Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space, let $C(X,{\mathbb{R}})$ be the set of real-valued continuous functions. Define

$$d(f,g) := \lVert {f-g} \rVert_X = \sup_{x \in X} \bigl\lvert {f(x)-g(x)} \bigr\rvert .$$

(a) Show that $d$ makes $C(X,{\mathbb{R}})$ into a metric space.

(b) Show that for every $x \in X$, the evaluation function $E_x \colon C(X,{\mathbb{R}}) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ defined by $E_x(f) := f(x)$ is a continuous function.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 13
q: Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, $S \subset X$, and $p \in X$. Prove that $p$ is a cluster point of $S$ if and only if $p \in \overline{S \setminus \{ p \}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 16
q:
Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces, $S \subset X$, $p \in X$ a cluster point of $S$, and let $f \colon S \to Y$ be a function. Prove that $f \colon S \to Y$ is continuous at $p$ if and only if

$$\lim_{x \to p} f(x) = f(p) .$$

title: Basic Analysis 7.5 · Exercise 17
q:
Define

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} \frac{2xy}{x^4+y^2} & \text{if } (x,y) \neq (0,0), \\ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) = (0,0) . \end{cases}$$

(a) Show that for every fixed $y$ the function that takes $x$ to $f(x,y)$ is continuous and hence Riemann integrable.

(b) For every fixed $x$, the function that takes $y$ to $f(x,y)$ is continuous.

(c) Show that $f$ is not continuous at $(0,0)$.

(d) Now show that $g(y) := \int_0^1 f(x,y)\,dx$ is not continuous at $y=0$.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about $\arctan$ from calculus, in particular that $\frac{d}{ds} \bigl[ \arctan(s) \bigr] = \frac{1}{1+s^2}$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 1
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q: Let $J$ be a closed and bounded interval and $Y := \bigl\{ f \in C\bigl([-h,h],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr) : f\bigl([-h,h]\bigr) \subset J \bigr\}$. Show that $Y \subset C\bigl([-h,h],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$ is closed. Hint: $J$ is closed.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 2
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
In the proof of Picard's theorem, show that if $f \colon [-h,h] \to J$ is continuous, then $F\bigl(t,f(t)\bigr)$ is continuous on $[-h,h]$ as a function of $t$. Use this to show that

$$T(f)(x) := y_0 + \int_0^x F\bigl(t,f(t)\bigr)\,dt$$

is well-defined and that $T(f) \in C\bigl([-h,h],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 3
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q: Prove that in the proof of Picard's theorem, the statement “Without loss of generality assume $x_0 = 0$” is justified. That is, prove that if we know the theorem with $x_0 = 0$, the theorem is true as stated.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 4
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
Let $F \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be defined by $F(x) := kx + b$ where $0 < k < 1$, $b \in {\mathbb{R}}$.

(a) Show that $F$ is a contraction.

(b) Find the fixed point and show directly that it is unique.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 5
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
Let $f \colon [0,{1}/{4}] \to [0,{1}/{4}]$ be defined by $f(x) := x^2$.

(a) Show that $f$ is a contraction, and find the best (smallest) $k$ from the definition that works.

(b) Find the fixed point and show directly that it is unique.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 6
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
(a) Find an example of a contraction $f \colon X \to X$ of a non-complete metric space $X$ with no fixed point.

(b) Find a 1-Lipschitz map $f \colon X \to X$ of a complete metric space $X$ with no fixed point.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 7
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q: Consider $y' =y^2$, $y(0)=1$. Use the iteration scheme from the proof of the contraction mapping principle. Start with $f_0(x) = 1$. Find a few iterates (at least up to $f_2$). Prove that the pointwise limit of $f_n$ is $\frac{1}{1-x}$, that is, for every $x$ with $\lvert {x} \rvert < h$ for some $h > 0$, prove that $\lim\limits_{n\to\infty}f_n(x) = \frac{1}{1-x}$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 8
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
Suppose $f \colon X \to X$ is a contraction for $k < 1$. Suppose you use the iteration procedure with $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$ as in the proof of the fixed point theorem. Suppose $x$ is the fixed point of $f$.

(a) Show that $d(x,x_n) \leq k^n d(x_1,x_0) \frac{1}{1-k}$ for all $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$.

(b) Suppose $d(y_1,y_2) \leq 16$ for all $y_1,y_2 \in X$, and $k= {1}/{2}$. Find an $N$ such that starting at any given point $x_0 \in X$, $d(x,x_n) \leq 2^{-16}$ for all $n \geq N$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 9
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q:
Let $f(x) := x-\frac{x^2-2}{2x}$ (you may recognize Newton's method for $\sqrt{2}$).

(a) Prove $f\bigl([1,\infty)\bigr) \subset [1,\infty)$.

(b) Prove that $f \colon [1,\infty) \to [1,\infty)$ is a contraction.

(c) Show that the fixed point theorem applies, find the unique $x \geq 1$ such that $f(x) = x$, and show that $x = \sqrt{2}$. Note: In particular, the technique from the proof of the theorem can be used to approximate $\sqrt{2}$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 10
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q: Suppose $f \colon X \to X$ is a contraction, and $(X,d)$ is a metric space with the discrete metric, that is, $d(x,y) = 1$ whenever $x \neq y$. Show that $f$ is constant, that is, there exists a $c \in X$ such that $f(x) = c$ for all $x \in X$.

title: Basic Analysis 7.6 · Exercise 11
section: §7.6 Fixed point theorem and Picard's theorem again
q: Suppose $(X,d)$ is a nonempty complete metric space, $f \colon X \to X$ is a mapping, and denote by $f^n$ the $n$th iterate of $f$. Suppose for every $n$ there exists a $k_n > 0$ such that $d\bigl(f^n(x),f^n(y)\bigr) \leq k_n \, d(x,y)$ for all $x,y \in X$, where $\sum_{n=1}^\infty k_n < \infty$. Prove that $f$ has a unique fixed point in $X$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 1
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Show that in ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ (with the standard euclidean metric), for every $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and every $r > 0$, the ball $B(x,r)$ is convex.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 2
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Verify that ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a vector space.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 3
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q:
Let $X$ be a vector space. Prove that a finite set of vectors $\{ x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \} \subset X$ is linearly independent if and only if for every $k=1,2,\ldots,n$

$$\operatorname{span}\bigl( \{ x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1},x_{k+1},\ldots,x_n \}\bigr) \subsetneq \operatorname{span}\bigl( \{ x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n \}\bigr) .$$

That is, the span of the set with one vector removed is strictly smaller.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 5
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Prove $C([0,1],{\mathbb{R}})$ is an infinite-dimensional vector space where the operations are defined in the obvious way: $s=f+g$ and $m=af$ are defined as $s(x) := f(x)+g(x)$ and $m(x) := a f(x)$. Hint: For the dimension, think of functions that are only nonzero on the interval $({1}/{n+1},{1}/{n})$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 6
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q:
Let $k \colon [0,1]^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be continuous. Show that $L \colon C([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}) \to C([0,1],{\mathbb{R}})$ defined by

$$Lf(y) := \int_0^1 k(x,y)f(x)\,dx$$

is a linear operator. That is, first show that $L$ is well-defined by showing that $Lf$ is continuous whenever $f$ is, and then showing that $L$ is linear.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 7
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Let ${\mathscr{P}}_n$ be the vector space of polynomials in one variable of degree $n$ or less. Show that ${\mathscr{P}}_n$ is a vector space of dimension $n+1$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 8
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Let ${\mathbb{R}}[t]$ be the vector space of polynomials in one variable $t$. Let $D \colon {\mathbb{R}}[t] \to {\mathbb{R}}[t]$ be the derivative operator (derivative in $t$). Show that $D$ is a linear operator.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 12
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q:
Suppose $X$ and $Y$ are vector spaces and $A \in L(X,Y)$ is a linear mapping.

(a) Show that the nullspace $N := \{ x \in X : Ax = 0 \}$ is a vector space.

(b) Show that the range $R := \{ y \in Y : Ax = y \text{ for some } x \in X \}$ is a vector space.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 13
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Show by example that a union of convex sets need not be convex.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 14
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Compute the convex hull of the set of 3 points $\bigl\{ (0,0), (0,1), (1,1) \bigr\}$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^2$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 15
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Show that the set $\bigl\{ (x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : y > x^2 \bigr\}$ is a convex set.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 17
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Show that every convex set in ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ is connected using the standard topology on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 18
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Suppose $K \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is a convex set such that the only point of the form $(x,0)$ in $K$ is the point $(0,0)$. Further suppose that $(0,1) \in K$ and $(1,1) \in K$. Show that if $(x,y) \in K$ and $x \neq 0$, then $y > 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.1 · Exercise 19
section: §8.1 Vector spaces, linear mappings, and convexity
q: Prove that an arbitrary intersection of vector subspaces is a vector subspace. That is, if $X$ is a vector space and $\{ V_\lambda \}_{\lambda \in I}$ is an arbitrary collection of vector subspaces of $X$, then $\bigcap_{\lambda \in I} V_\lambda$ is a vector subspace of $X$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 1
q: For a vector space $X$ with a norm $\lVert {\cdot} \rVert$, show that $d(x,y) := \lVert {x-y} \rVert$ makes $X$ a metric space.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 2
q: Show that for square matrices $A$ and $B$, $\det(AB) = \det(BA)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 3
q:
For $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$, define

$$\lVert {x} \rVert_{\infty} := \max \bigl\{ \lvert {x_1} \rvert, \lvert {x_2} \rvert, \ldots, \lvert {x_n} \rvert \bigr\} ,$$

sometimes called the sup or the max norm.

(a) Show that $\lVert {\cdot} \rVert_\infty$ is a norm on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ (defining a different distance).

(b) What is the unit ball $B(0,1)$ in this norm?

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 4
q:
For $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$, define

$$\lVert {x} \rVert_{1} := \sum_{k=1}^n \lvert {x_k} \rvert,$$

sometimes called the $1$-norm (or $L^1$ norm).

(a) Show that $\lVert {\cdot} \rVert_1$ is a norm on ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ (defining a different distance, sometimes called the taxicab distance).

(b) What is the unit ball $B(0,1)$ in this norm? Think about what it is in ${\mathbb{R}}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$. Hint: It is, for example, a convex hull of a finite number of points.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 5
q:
Using the euclidean norm on ${\mathbb{R}}^2$, compute the operator norm of the operators in $L({\mathbb{R}}^2)$ given by the matrices:

a) $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$

b) $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$

c) $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$

d) $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{smallmatrix} \right]$

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 6
q:
Using the standard euclidean norm ${\mathbb{R}}^n$, show:

(a) Suppose $A \in L({\mathbb{R}},{\mathbb{R}}^n)$ is defined for $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$ by $Ax := xa$ for a vector $a \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$. Then the operator norm $\lVert {A} \rVert_{L({\mathbb{R}},{\mathbb{R}}^n)} = \lVert {a} \rVert_{{\mathbb{R}}^n}$. (That is, the operator norm of $A$ is the euclidean norm of $a$.)

(b) Suppose $B \in L({\mathbb{R}}^n,{\mathbb{R}})$ is defined for $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ by $Bx := b \cdot x$ for a vector $b \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$. Then the operator norm $\lVert {B} \rVert_{L({\mathbb{R}}^n,{\mathbb{R}})} = \lVert {b} \rVert_{{\mathbb{R}}^n}$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 8
q: Verify the computation of the determinant for the three types of elementary matrices.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 10
q:
(a) Suppose $D = [d_{i,j}]$ is an $n$-by-$n$ diagonal matrix, that is, $d_{i,j} = 0$ whenever $i \neq j$. Show that $\det(D) = d_{1,1}d_{2,2} \cdots d_{n,n}$.

(b) Suppose $A$ is a diagonalizable matrix. That is, there exists a matrix $B$ such that $B^{-1}AB = D$ for a diagonal matrix $D = [d_{i,j}]$. Show that $\det(A) = d_{1,1}d_{2,2} \cdots d_{n,n}$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 14
q: Let $A$ be an upper triangular matrix. Find a formula for the determinant of $A$ in terms of the diagonal entries, and prove that your formula works.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 15
q: Given an $n$-by-$n$ matrix $A$, prove that $\bigl\lvert {\det(A)} \bigr\rvert \leq \lVert {A} \rVert^n$ (the norm on $A$ is the operator norm). Hint: One way to do it is to first prove it in the case $\lVert {A} \rVert=1$, which means that all columns are of norm 1 or less, then prove that this means that $\bigl\lvert {\det(A)} \bigr\rvert \leq 1$ using linearity.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 17
q: Let $A,S$ be $n$-by-$n$ matrices, where $S$ is invertible. Prove that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, if and only if it is an eigenvalue of $S^{-1}AS$. Then prove that $\rho(S^{-1}AS) = \rho(A)$. In particular, $\rho$ is a well-defined function on $L(X)$ for every finite-dimensional vector space $X$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.2 · Exercise 18
q:
Let $A$ be an $n$-by-$n$ matrix.

(a) Prove $\rho(A) \leq \lVert {A} \rVert$. (See above for definition of $\rho$.)

(b) For every $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$, prove $\rho(A) \leq \lVert {A^k} \rVert^{1/k}$.

(c) Suppose $\displaystyle \lim_{k\to\infty} A^k = 0$ (limit in the operator norm). Prove that $\rho(A) < 1$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 1
q:
Suppose $\gamma \colon (-1,1) \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\alpha \colon (-1,1) \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are two differentiable curves such that $\gamma(0) = \alpha(0)$ and $\gamma'(0) = \alpha'(0)$. Suppose $F \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a differentiable function. Show that

$$\frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F\bigl(\gamma(t)\bigr) = \frac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=0} F\bigl(\alpha(t)\bigr) .$$

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 3
q:
Using only the definition of the derivative, show that the following $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ are differentiable at the origin and find their derivative.

(a) $f(x,y) := (1+x+xy,x)$,

(b) $f(x,y) := \bigl(y-y^{10},x \bigr)$,

(c) $f(x,y) := \bigl( {(x+y+1)}^2 , {(x-y+2)}^2 \bigr)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 4
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $g \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are differentiable functions. Using only the definition of the derivative, show that $h \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ defined by $h(x,y) := \bigl(f(x),g(y)\bigr)$ is a differentiable function, and find the derivative, at all points $(x,y)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 7
q:
Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is one-to-one, onto, differentiable at all points, and such that $f^{-1}$ is also differentiable at all points.

(a) Show that $f'(p)$ is invertible at all points $p$ and compute ${(f^{-1})}'\bigl(f(p)\bigr)$. Hint: Consider $x = f^{-1}\bigl(f(x)\bigr)$.

(b) Let $g \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be a function differentiable at $q \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and such that $g(q)=q$. Suppose $f(p) = q$ for some $p \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$. Show $J_g(q) = J_{f^{-1} \circ g \circ f}(p)$ where $J_g$ is the Jacobian determinant.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 8
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is differentiable and such that $f(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $y=0$ and such that $\nabla f(0,0) = (0,1)$. Prove that $f(x,y) > 0$ whenever $y > 0$, and $f(x,y) < 0$ whenever $y < 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 9
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is differentiable. Suppose $f$ has a relative maximum at $p \in U$. Show that $f'(p) = 0$, that is, the zero mapping in $L({\mathbb{R}}^n,{\mathbb{R}})$. Namely, $p$ is a critical point of $f$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 10
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is differentiable and $f(x,y) = 0$ whenever $x^2+y^2 = 1$. Prove that there exists at least one point $(x_0,y_0)$ such that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0) = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 12
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is differentiable and $\bigl\lVert {f(t)} \bigr\rVert = 1$ for all $t$ (that is, we have a curve in the unit sphere). Show that $f'(t) \cdot f(t) = 0$ (treating $f'(t)$ as a vector) for all $t$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 13
q: Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ by $f(x,y) := \bigl(x,y+\varphi(x)\bigr)$ for some differentiable function $\varphi$ of one variable. Show $f$ is differentiable and find $f'$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 14
q:
Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open, $p \in U$, and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$, $g \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$, $h \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are functions such that $f(p) = g(p) = h(p)$, $f$ and $h$ are differentiable at $p$, $f'(p) = h'(p)$, and

$$f(x) \leq g(x) \leq h(x) \qquad \text{for all } x \in U .$$

Show that $g$ is differentiable at $p$ and $g'(p) = f'(p) = h'(p)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 15
q: Prove a version of the mean value theorem for functions of several variables. That is, suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open, $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ differentiable, $p,q \in U$, and the segment $[p,q] \in U$. Prove that there exists an $x \in [p,q]$ such that $\nabla f (x) \cdot (q-p) = f(q)-f(p)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.3 · Exercise 16
q: Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by $f(x,y) := \frac{y(x^2+y^2)}{x}$ when $x \neq 0$ and $f(0,y) := 0$. Show that for all $u \in {\mathbb{R}}^2$ with $\lVert {u} \rVert=1$, we get $D_u f(0) = 0$, that is, the directional derivative exists and is zero in all directions at the origin, but the function is not continuous at the origin (in fact, not continuous whenever $x=0$).

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 1
q:
Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ as

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} (x^2+y^2)\sin\bigl({(x^2+y^2)}^{-1}\bigr) & \text{if } (x,y) \neq (0,0), \\ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) = (0,0). \end{cases}$$

Show that $f$ is differentiable at the origin, but that it is not continuously differentiable.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 3
q:
Let $B(0,1) \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ be the unit ball, that is, the set given by $x^2 + y^2 < 1$. Suppose $f \colon B(0,1) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a differentiable function such that $\bigl\lvert {f(0,0)} \bigr\rvert \leq 1$, and $\bigl\lvert {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}} \bigr\rvert \leq 1$ and $\bigl\lvert {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} \bigr\rvert \leq 1$ for all points in $B(0,1)$.

(a) Find an $M \in {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\bigl\lVert {f'(x,y)} \bigr\rVert \leq M$ for all $(x,y) \in B(0,1)$.

(b) Find a $B \in {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\bigl\lvert {f(x,y)} \bigr\rvert \leq B$ for all $(x,y) \in B(0,1)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 4
q: Define $\varphi \colon [0,2\pi] \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ by $\varphi(t) = \bigl(\sin(t),\cos(t)\bigr)$. Compute $\varphi'(t)$ for all $t$. Compute $\bigl\lVert {\varphi'(t)} \bigr\rVert$ for all $t$. Notice that $\varphi'(t)$ is never zero, yet $\varphi(0) = \varphi(2\pi)$. Therefore, Rolle's theorem is not true for vector-valued functions.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 5
q: Let $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be a function such that $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exist at all points and there exists an $M \in {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\bigl\lvert {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}} \bigr\rvert \leq M$ and $\bigl\lvert {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} \bigr\rvert \leq M$ at all points. Show that $f$ is continuous.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 6
q:
Let $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be a function and $M \in {\mathbb{R}}$, such that for every $(x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2$ with $x^2+y^2=1$, the function $g(t) := f(xt,yt)$ is differentiable and $\bigl\lvert {g'(t)} \bigr\rvert \leq M$ for all $t$.

(a) Show that $f$ is continuous at $(0,0)$.

(b) Find an example of such an $f$ that is discontinuous at every other point of ${\mathbb{R}}^2$.

Hint: Think back to how we constructed a nowhere continuous function on $[0,1]$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 7
q: Suppose $r \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \setminus X \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a rational function, that is, $p \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $q \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are polynomials, $q$ is not identically zero, $X = q^{-1}(0)$, and $r = \frac{p}{q}$. Show that $r$ is continuously differentiable.

title: Basic Analysis 8.4 · Exercise 8
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $h \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are two differentiable functions such that $f'(x) = h'(x)$ for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$. Prove that if $f(0) = h(0)$, then $f(x) = h(x)$ for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}^n$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 1
q:
Let $C := \bigl\{ (x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : x^2+y^2 = 1 \bigr\}$.

(a) Solve for $y$ in terms of $x$ near $(0,1)$ (that is, find the function $g$ from the implicit function theorem for a neighborhood of the point $(p,q) = (0,1)$).

(b) Solve for $y$ in terms of $x$ near $(0,-1)$.

(c) Solve for $x$ in terms of $y$ near $(-1,0)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 2
q:
Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ by $f(x,y) := \bigl(x,y+h(x)\bigr)$ for some continuously differentiable function $h$ of one variable.

(a) Show that $f$ is one-to-one and onto.

(b) Compute $f'$. (Make sure to argue why $f'$ exists.)

(c) Show that $f'$ is invertible at all points and compute its inverse.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 3
q:
Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus \bigl\{ (0,0) \bigr\}$ by $f(x,y) := \bigl(e^x\cos(y),e^x\sin(y)\bigr)$.

(a) Show that $f$ is onto.

(b) Show that $f'$ is invertible at all points.

(c) Show that $f$ is not one-to-one, in fact for every $(a,b) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus \bigl\{ (0,0) \bigr\}$, there exist infinitely many different points $(x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2$ such that $f(x,y) = (a,b)$.

Therefore, invertible derivative at every point does not mean that $f$ is invertible globally.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 4
q: Find a map $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ that is one-to-one, onto, continuously differentiable, but $f'(0) = 0$. Hint: Generalize $f(x) = x^3$ from one to $n$ dimensions.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 5
q: Consider $z^2 + xz + y =0$ in ${\mathbb{R}}^3$. Find an equation $D(x,y)=0$, such that if $D(x_0,y_0) \neq 0$ and $z^2+x_0z+y_0 = 0$ for some $z \in {\mathbb{R}}$, then for points near $(x_0,y_0)$ there exist exactly two distinct continuously differentiable functions $r_1(x,y)$ and $r_2(x,y)$ such that $z=r_1(x,y)$ and $z=r_2(x,y)$ solve $z^2 + xz + y =0$. Do you recognize the expression $D$ from algebra?

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose $f \colon (a,b) \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is continuously differentiable and the first component (the $x$ component) of $\nabla f(t)$ is not equal to 0 for all $t \in (a,b)$. Prove that there exists an open interval $I \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ and a continuously differentiable function $g \colon I \to {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $(x,y) \in f\bigl((a,b)\bigr)$ if and only if $x \in I$ and $y=g(x)$. In other words, the set $f\bigl((a,b)\bigr)$ is a graph of $g$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 7
q:
Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} \bigl(x^2 \sin ({1}/{x}) + {x}/{2} , y \bigr) & \text{if } x \neq 0, \\ (0,y) & \text{if } x=0. \end{cases}$$

(a) Show that $f$ is differentiable everywhere.

(b) Show that $f'(0,0)$ is invertible.

(c) Show that $f$ is not one-to-one in every neighborhood of the origin (it is not locally invertible, that is, the inverse function theorem does not work).

(d) Show that $f$ is not continuously differentiable.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 9
q:
Let $H := \bigl\{ (x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : y > 0 \}$, and for $(x,y) \in H$ define

$$F(x,y) := \left( \frac{x^2+y^2-1}{x^2+2y+y^2+1} ,~ \frac{-2x}{x^2+2y+y^2+1} \right) .$$

Prove that $F$ is a bijective mapping from $H$ to $B(0,1)$, it is continuously differentiable on $H$, and its inverse is also continuously differentiable.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 10
q:
Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is open and $f \colon U 	o {\mathbb{R}}$ is a $C^1$ function such that $
abla f(x,y) 
eq 0$ for all $(x,y) \in U$. Show that every level set is a $C^1$ smooth curve. That is, for every $(x,y) \in U$, there exists a $C^1$ function $\gamma \colon (-\delta,\delta) 	o {\mathbb{R}}^2$ with $\gamma'(0) 
eq 0$ such that $f igl(\gamma(t) igr)$ is constant for all $t \in (-\delta,\delta)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.5 · Exercise 11
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is open and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a $C^1$ function such that $\nabla f(x,y) \neq 0$ for all $(x,y) \in U$. Show that for every $(x,y)$ there exists a neighborhood $V$ of $(x,y)$ an open set $W \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$, a bijective $C^1$ function with a $C^1$ inverse $g \colon W \to V$ such that the level sets of $f \circ g$ are horizontal lines in $W$, that is, the set given by $(f \circ g) (s,t) = c$ for a constant $c$ is a set of the form $\bigl\{ (s,t_0) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : s \in {\mathbb{R}}, (s,t_0) \in W \bigr\}$, where $t_0$ is fixed. That is, the level curves can be locally “straightened.”

title: Basic Analysis 8.6 · Exercise 2
q:
Define

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} \frac{xy(x^2-y^2)}{x^2+y^2} & \text{if } (x,y) \neq (0,0),\\ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) = (0,0). \end{cases}$$

Show that

(a) The first order partial derivatives exist and are continuous.

(b) The partial derivatives $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y}$ and $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}$ exist, but are not continuous at $(0,0)$, and $\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x \partial y}(0,0) \neq \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y \partial x}(0,0)$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.6 · Exercise 3
q:
Let $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be a $C^k$ function for some open $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $p \in U$. Suppose ${\ell}_1,{\ell}_2,\ldots,{\ell}_k$ are integers between $1$ and $n$, and $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\ldots,\sigma_k)$ is a permutation of $(1,2,\ldots,k)$. Prove

$$\frac{\partial^{k} f}{\partial x_{{\ell}_{k}} \partial x_{{\ell}_{k-1}} \cdots \partial x_{{\ell}_1}} (p) = \frac{\partial^{k} f}{\partial x_{{\ell}_{\sigma_k}} \partial x_{{\ell}_{\sigma_{k-1}}} \cdots \partial x_{{\ell}_{\sigma_1}}} (p) .$$

title: Basic Analysis 8.6 · Exercise 5
q:
Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a $C^2$ function. For all $(x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2$, compute

$$\lim_{t \to 0} \frac{f(x+t,y)+f(x-t,y)+f(x,y+t)+f(x,y-t) - 4f(x,y)}{t^2}$$

in terms of the partial derivatives of $f$.

title: Basic Analysis 8.6 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a function such that all first and second order partial derivatives exist. Furthermore, suppose that all second order partial derivatives are bounded functions. Prove that $f$ is continuously differentiable.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 2
q:
Suppose $h \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuous and $g \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuously differentiable and compactly supported. That is, there exists some $M > 0$, such that $g(x) = 0$ whenever $\lvert {x} \rvert \geq M$. Define

$$f(x) := \int_{-\infty}^\infty h(y)g(x-y)\,dy .$$

Show that $f$ is differentiable.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 3
q:
Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is infinitely differentiable (derivatives of all orders exist) and $f(0) = 0$. Show that there exists an infinitely differentiable function $g \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $f(x) = x\,g(x)$. Show also that if $f'(0) \neq 0$, then $g(0) \neq 0$.

Hint: Write $f(x) = \int_0^x f'(s) \,ds$ and then rewrite the integral to go from $0$ to $1$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 4
q: Compute $\int_0^1 e^{tx} \,dx$. Derive the formula for $\int_0^1 x^n e^{x} \,dx$ not using integration by parts, but by differentiation underneath the integral.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 5
q:
Let $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be open and suppose $f(x,y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)$ is a continuous function defined on $[0,1] \times U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$. Suppose $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y_1}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_2},\ldots, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y_n}$ exist and are continuous on $[0,1] \times U$. Prove that $F \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ defined by

$$F(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n) := \int_0^1 f(x,y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n) \, dx$$

is continuously differentiable.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 7
q:
Work out the following counterexample: Let

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} x \,\sin \left(\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}\right) & \text{if } (x,y) \neq (0,0),\\ 0 & \text{if } (x,y)=(0,0). \end{cases}$$

(a) Prove $f$ is continuous on all of ${\mathbb{R}}^2$. Therefore the following function is well-defined for every $y \in {\mathbb{R}}$:

$$g(y) := \int_0^1 f(x,y) \, dx .$$

(b) Prove $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ exists for all $(x,y)$, but is not continuous at $(0,0)$.

(c) Show that $\int_0^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,0) \, dx$ does not exist even if we take improper integrals, that is, that the limit $\lim\limits_{h \to 0^+} \int_h^1 \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x,0) \, dx$ does not exist.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 9.1 · Exercise 9
q:
Suppose $g \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuously differentiable, $h \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuous, $\frac{\partial h}{\partial x}$ exists and is continuous at all points. Show that

$$F(x,y) := g(x) + \int_0^y h(x,s) \,ds$$

is continuously differentiable, and that it is the solution of the partial differential equation $\frac{\partial F}{\partial y} = h$, with the initial condition $F(x,0) = g(x)$ for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 1
q: Show that if $\varphi \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a piecewise smooth path as we defined it, then $\varphi$ is a continuous function.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose $\gamma \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a piecewise smooth path, and $f$ is a continuous function defined on the image $\gamma\bigl([a,b]\bigr)$. Provide a definition of $\int_{\gamma} f \,ds$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 8
q: Suppose $\gamma \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a smooth path, and $\omega$ is a one-form defined on the image $\gamma\bigl([a,b]\bigr)$. For $r \in [0,1]$, let $\gamma_r \colon [0,r] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be defined as simply the restriction of $\gamma$ to $[0,r]$. Show that the function $h(r) := \int_{\gamma_r} \omega$ is a continuously differentiable function on $[0,1]$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 9
q: Suppose $\gamma \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a smooth path. Show that there exists an $\epsilon > 0$ and a continuously differentiable function $\widetilde{\gamma} \colon (a-\epsilon,b+\epsilon) \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) = \gamma(t)$ for all $t \in [a,b]$ and $\widetilde{\gamma}'(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in (a-\epsilon,b+\epsilon)$. That is, prove that a smooth path extends some small distance past the end points.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 10
q: Suppose $\alpha \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\beta \colon [c,d] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are piecewise smooth paths such that $\Gamma := \alpha\bigl([a,b]\bigr) = \beta\bigl([c,d]\bigr)$. Show that there exist finitely many points $\{ p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k\} \in \Gamma$, such that the sets $\alpha^{-1}\bigl( \{ p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k\} \bigr)$ and $\beta^{-1}\bigl( \{ p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_k\} \bigr)$ are partitions of $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ such that on every subinterval the paths are smooth (that is, they are partitions as in the definition of piecewise smooth path).

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 12
q:
Suppose $\alpha \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\beta \colon [b,c] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are piecewise smooth paths with $\alpha(b)=\beta(b)$. Let $\gamma \colon [a,c] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be defined by

$$\gamma(t) := \begin{cases} \alpha(t) & \text{if } t \in [a,b], \\ \beta(t) & \text{if } t \in (b,c]. \end{cases}$$

Show that $\gamma$ is a piecewise smooth path, and that if $\omega$ is a one-form defined on the curve given by $\gamma$, then

$$\int_{\gamma} \omega = \int_{\alpha} \omega + \int_{\beta} \omega .$$

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 13
q:
Suppose $\gamma \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\beta \colon [c,d] \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are two simple closed piecewise smooth paths. That is, $\gamma(a)=\gamma(b)$ and $\beta(c) = \beta(d)$ and the restrictions $\gamma|_{[a,b)}$ and $\beta|_{[c,d)}$ are one-to-one. Suppose $\Gamma = \gamma\bigl([a,b]\bigr) = \beta\bigl([c,d]\bigr)$ and $\omega$ is a one-form defined on $\Gamma \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$. Show that either

$$\int_\gamma \omega = \int_\beta \omega, \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_\gamma \omega = - \int_\beta \omega.$$

In particular, the notation $\int_{\Gamma} \omega$ makes sense if we indicate the direction in which the integral is evaluated. Hint: See previous three exercises.

title: Basic Analysis 9.2 · Exercise 15
q:
Define $\gamma \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}^2$ by $\gamma(t) := \Bigl( t^3 \sin({1}/{t}),\, t{\bigl(3t^2\sin({1}/{t})-t\cos({1}/{t})\bigr)}^2 \Bigr)$ for $t \neq 0$ and $\gamma(0) = (0,0)$. Show that

(a) $\gamma$ is continuously differentiable on $[0,1]$.

(b) Show that there exists an infinite sequence $\{ t_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ in $[0,1]$ converging to 0, such that $\gamma'(t_n) = (0,0)$.

(c) Show that the points $\gamma(t_n)$ lie on the line $y=0$ and such that the $x$-coordinate of $\gamma(t_n)$ alternates between positive and negative (if they do not alternate you only found a subsequence, you need to find them all).

(d) Show that there is no piecewise smooth path $\alpha$ whose image equals $\gamma\bigl([0,1]\bigr)$. Hint: Look at part c) and show that $\alpha'$ must be zero where it reaches the origin.

(e) (Computer) If you know a plotting software that allows you to plot parametric curves, make a plot of the curve, but only for $t$ in the range $[0,0.1]$ otherwise you will not see the behavior. In particular, you should notice that $\gamma\bigl([0,1]\bigr)$ has infinitely many “corners” near the origin.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 1
q: Find an $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $df = xe^{x^2+y^2}\, dx + ye^{x^2+y^2} \, dy$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 2
q: Find an $\omega_2 \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ such that there exists a continuously differentiable $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ for which $df = e^{xy} \,dx + \omega_2 \,dy$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 4
q: Show that if $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a star-shaped domain, then it is path connected.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 5
q: Show that $U := {\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus \{ (x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : x \leq 0, y=0 \}$ is a star-shaped domain and find all points $(x_0,y_0) \in U$ such that $U$ is star-shaped with respect to $(x_0,y_0)$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose $U_1$ and $U_2$ are two open sets in ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ with $U_1 \cap U_2$ nonempty and path connected. Suppose there exists an $f_1 \colon U_1 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $f_2 \colon U_2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$, both twice continuously differentiable such that $d f_1 = d f_2$ on $U_1 \cap U_2$. Then there exists a twice differentiable function $F \colon U_1 \cup U_2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $dF = df_1$ on $U_1$ and $dF = df_2$ on $U_2$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 9
q:
Usually path connectedness is defined using continuous paths rather than piecewise smooth paths. Prove that for open subsets of ${\mathbb{R}}^n$ the definitions are equivalent, in other words prove:

Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open and for every $x,y \in U$, there exists a continuous function $\gamma \colon [a,b] \to U$ such that $\gamma(a) = x$ and $\gamma(b) = y$. Then $U$ is path connected, that is, there is a piecewise smooth path in $U$ from $x$ to $y$.

title: Basic Analysis 9.3 · Exercise 10
q:
Take

$$\omega(x,y) := \frac{-y}{x^2+y^2} \, dx + \frac{x}{x^2+y^2} \, dy$$

defined on ${\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus \{ (0,0) \}$. Let $\gamma \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus \{ (0,0) \}$ be a closed piecewise smooth path. Let $R := \{ (x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2 : x \leq 0 \text{ and } y=0 \}$. Suppose $R \cap \gamma\bigl([a,b]\bigr)$ is a finite set of $k$ points. Prove that

$$\int_{\gamma} \omega = 2 \pi \ell$$

for some integer $\ell$ with $\lvert {\ell} \rvert \leq k$.

Hint 1: First prove that for a path $\beta$ that starts and end on $R$ but does not intersect it otherwise, you find that $\int_{\beta} \omega$ is $-2\pi$, 0, or $2\pi$.

Hint 2: You proved above that ${\mathbb{R}}^2 \setminus R$ is star-shaped.

Note: The number $\ell$ is called the winding number it measures how many times $\gamma$ winds around the origin in the counterclockwise direction.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 1
q:
Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuous and of compact support. Show that the function $\widetilde{f} \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$, where

$$\widetilde{f}(x) := \begin{cases} f(x) & \text{if } x \in U, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} $$

is continuous.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 3
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle with the length of one of the sides equal to 0. For every bounded function $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$, show that $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$ and $\int_R f = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 4
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle with the length of one of the sides equal to 0, and suppose $S$ is a closed rectangle with $R \subset S$. If $f \colon S \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a bounded function such that $f(x) = 0$ for $x \in S \setminus R$, show that $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(S)$ and $\int_S f = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 5
q: Suppose $f\colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is such that $f(x) := 0$ if $x \neq 0$ and $f(0) := 1$. Show that $f$ is integrable on $R := [-1,1] \times [-1,1] \times \cdots \times [-1,1]$ directly using the definition, and find $\int_R f$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 10
q: Suppose $R$ and $S$ are closed rectangles in ${\mathbb{R}}^n$. Define $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ as $f(x) := 1$ if $x \in R$, and $f(x) := 0$ otherwise. Prove $f$ is integrable on $S$ and compute $\int_S f$. Hint: Consider $S \cap R$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 11
q:
Let $R := [0,1] \times [0,1] \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$.

(a) Suppose $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is defined by

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x = y, \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

Show that $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$ and compute $\int_R f$.

(b) Suppose $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is defined by

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } x \in {\mathbb{Q}} \text{ or } y \in {\mathbb{Q}}, \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

Show that $f \notin {\mathscr{R}}(R)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 12
q:
Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle, and suppose $\{ S_j \}_{j=1}^\infty$ is a sequence of closed rectangles such that $S_j \subset R$ and $S_j \subset S_{j+1}$ for all $j$, and also $R = \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty S_j$. Suppose $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is bounded and $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(S_j)$ for all $j$. Show that $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$ and

$$\lim_{j\to\infty} \int_{S_j} f = \int_R f .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.1 · Exercise 13
q:
Suppose $f\colon [-1,1] \times [-1,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a Riemann integrable function where $f(x) = -f(-x)$. Using the definition of the integral prove

$$\int_{[-1,1] \times [-1,1]} f = 0 .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 1
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q: Compute $\int_{0}^1 \int_{-1}^1 xe^{xy} \, dx \, dy$ in a simple way.

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 4
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Let $R := [a,b] \times [c,d]$ and $f(x,y)$ be an integrable function on $R$ such that for every fixed $y$, the function that takes $x$ to $f(x,y)$ is zero except at finitely many points. Show

$$\int_R f = 0 .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 5
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Let $R := [a,b] \times [c,d]$ and $f(x,y) := g(x)h(y)$ for continuous functions $g \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $h \colon [c,d] \to {\mathbb{R}}$. Prove

$$\int_R f = \left(\int_a^b g\right)\left(\int_c^d h\right) .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 6
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Compute (using calculus)

$$\int_0^1 \int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{{(x^2+y^2)}^2} \, dx \, dy \qquad \text{and} \qquad \int_0^1 \int_0^1 \frac{x^2-y^2}{{(x^2+y^2)}^2} \, dy \, dx .$$

You will need to interpret the integrals as improper, that is, the limit of $\int_\epsilon^1$ as $\epsilon \to 0^+$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 7
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Suppose $f(x,y) := g(x)$ where $g \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is Riemann integrable. Show that $f$ is Riemann integrable for every $R = [a,b] \times [c,d]$ and

$$\int_R f = (d-c) \int_a^b g .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 8
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Define $f \colon [-1,1] \times [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} x & \text{if } y \in {\mathbb{Q}}, \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

(a) Show $\int_0^1 \int_{-1}^1 f(x,y) \, dx \, dy$ exists, but $\int_{-1}^1 \int_0^1 f(x,y) \, dy \, dx$ does not.

(b) Compute $\int_{-1}^1 \overline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dy \, dx$ and $\int_{-1}^1 \underline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dy \, dx$.

(c) Show $f$ is not Riemann integrable on $[-1,1] \times [0,1]$ (use Fubini).

title: Basic Analysis 10.2 · Exercise 9
section: §10.2 Iterated integrals and the Fubini theorem
q:
Define $f \colon [0,1] \times [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} {1}/{q} & \text{if } x \in {\mathbb{Q}}, y \in {\mathbb{Q}}, \text{ and } y={p}/{q} \text{ in lowest terms,} \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

(a) Show $f$ is Riemann integrable on $[0,1] \times [0,1]$.

(b) Find $\overline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dx$ and $\underline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dx$ for all $y \in [0,1]$, and show they are unequal for all $y \in {\mathbb{Q}}$.

(c) Show $\int_0^1 \int_0^1 f(x,y) \, dy \, dx$ exists, but $\int_0^1 \int_0^1 f(x,y) \, dx \, dy$ does not.

Note: By Fubini, $\int_0^1 \overline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy$ and $\int_0^1 \underline{\int_0^1} f(x,y) \, dx \, dy$ exist and equal $\int_{[0,1]\times[0,1]} f$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 2
q: If $A \subset B$, then $m^*(A) \leq m^*(B)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 3
q: Suppose $X \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a set such that for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a set $Y$ such that $X \subset Y$ and $m^*(Y) \leq \epsilon$. Prove that $X$ is a measure zero set.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 4
q: Show that if $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle, then $m^*(R) = V(R)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 5
q: The closure of a measure zero set can be quite large. Find an example set $S \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ that is of measure zero, but whose closure $\overline{S} = {\mathbb{R}}^n$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 7
q: Let $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be an open set and let $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be a continuously differentiable function. Let $G := \bigl\{ (x,y) \in U \times {\mathbb{R}} : y = f(x) \bigr\}$ be the graph of $f$. Show that $G$ is of measure zero.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 8
q:
Given a closed rectangle $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$, show that for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a number $s > 0$ and finitely many open cubes $C_1,C_2,\ldots,C_k$ of side $s$ such that $R \subset C_1 \cup C_2 \cup \cdots \cup C_k$ and

$$\sum_{j=1}^k V(C_j) \leq V(R) + \epsilon .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 9
q: Show that there exists a number $k = k(n,r,\delta)$ depending only on $n$, $r$, and $\delta$ such that the following holds: Given $B(x,r) \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $\delta > 0$, there exist $k$ open balls $B_1,B_2,\ldots,B_k$ of radius at most $\delta$ such that $B(x,r) \subset B_1 \cup B_2 \cup \cdots \cup B_k$. Note that you can find $k$ that only depends on $n$ and the ratio ${\delta}/{r}$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 13
q: Prove that we obtain the same outer measure if we allow both finite and infinite sequences in the definition. That is, define $\mu^*(S) := \inf\, \sum_{j \in I} V(R_j)$ where the infimum is taken over all countable (finite or infinite) sets of open rectangles $\{ R_j \}_{j\in I}$ such that $S \subset \bigcup_{j \in I} R_j$. Prove that for every $S \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$, $\mu^*(S) = m^*(S)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 14
q: Prove that for any two subsets $A, B \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$, we have $m^*(A \cup B) \leq m^*(A)+m^*(B)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 15
q: Suppose $A, B \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are such that $m^*(B)=0$. Prove that $m^*(A \cup B) = m^*(A)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.3 · Exercise 16
q: Suppose $R_1,R_2,\ldots,R_n$ are pairwise disjoint open rectangles. Prove that $m^*(R_1 \cup R_2 \cup \cdots \cup R_n) = m^*(R_1)+m^*(R_2)+\cdots+m^*(R_n)$. Hint: Some of the exercises above may prove very useful.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 1
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Suppose $f \colon (a,b) \times (c,d) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a bounded continuous function. Show that the integral of $f$ over $R = [a,b] \times [c,d]$ makes sense and is uniquely defined. That is, set $f$ to be anything (bounded) on the boundary of $R$ and compute the integral, showing that the values on the boundary are irrelevant.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 2
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle. Show that ${\mathscr{R}}(R)$, the set of Riemann integrable functions, is an algebra. That is, show that if $f,g \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$ and $a \in {\mathbb{R}}$, then $af \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$, $f+g \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$, and $fg \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 3
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a bounded function which is zero except on a closed set $E \subset R$ of measure zero. Show that $\int_R f$ exists and compute it.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 4
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $g \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are two Riemann integrable functions. Suppose $f = g$ except for a closed set $E \subset R$ of measure zero. Show that $\int_R f = \int_R g$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 5
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a bounded function.

(a) Suppose there exists a closed set $E \subset R$ of measure zero such that $f|_{R\setminus E}$ is continuous. Then $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(R)$.

(b) Find an example where $E \subset R$ is a set of measure zero (not closed) such that $f|_{R\setminus E}$ is continuous and $f \notin {\mathscr{R}}(R)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 6
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $g \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are Riemann integrable. Show that

$$\varphi(x) := \max \bigl\{ f(x) , g(x) \bigr\} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \psi(x) := \min \bigl\{ f(x) , g(x) \bigr\}$$

are Riemann integrable.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 7
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is Riemann integrable. Show that $\lvert {f} \rvert$ is Riemann integrable. Hint: Define $f_+(x) := \max \bigl\{ f(x) , 0 \bigr\}$ and $f_-(x) := \max \bigl\{ -f(x) , 0 \bigr\}$, and then write $\lvert {f} \rvert$ in terms of $f_+$ and $f_-$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 8
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
(a) Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $R' \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are closed rectangles, $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and $U' \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ are open sets such that $R \subset U$ and $R' \subset U'$, $g \colon U \to U'$ is continuously differentiable, bijective, $g^{-1}$ is continuously differentiable, $g(R) \subset R'$, and $f \in {\mathscr{R}}(R')$. Show that the composition $f \circ g$ is Riemann integrable on $R$.

(b) Find a counterexample when $g$ is not one-to-one. Hint: Try $g(x,y) := (x,0)$ and $R=R'=[0,1] \times [0,1]$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 9
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Suppose $f \colon [0,1]^2 \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is defined by

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} \frac{1}{kq} & \text{if } x,y \in {\mathbb{Q}} \text{ and } x = \frac{\ell}{k} \text{ and } y=\frac{p}{q} \text{ in lowest terms,} \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

Show that $f \in {\mathscr{R}}\bigl({[0,1]}^2\bigr)$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 10
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Compute the oscillation $o\bigl(f,(x,y)\bigr)$ for all $(x,y) \in {\mathbb{R}}^2$ for the function

$$f(x,y) := \begin{cases} \frac{xy}{x^2+y^2} & \text{if } (x,y) \neq (0,0), \\ 0 & \text{if } (x,y) = (0,0) . \end{cases}$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 11
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Consider the popcorn function $f \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$,

$$f(x) := \begin{cases} \frac{1}{q} & \text{if } x \in {\mathbb{Q}} \text{ and } x = \frac{p}{q} \text{ in lowest terms,} \\ 0 & \text{else.} \end{cases}$$

Compute $o(f,x)$ for all $x \in [0,1]$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 12
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q:
Suppose $f \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ and $g \colon [c,d] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are Riemann integrable. Show that $h \colon [a,b] \times [c,d] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ defined by $h(x,y) := f(x) g(y)$ is Riemann integrable and

$$\int_{[a,b] \times [c,d]} h = \left( \int_a^b f \right) \left( \int_c^d g \right) .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.4 · Exercise 13
section: §10.4 The set of Riemann integrable functions
q: Let $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ be a closed rectangle and $f \colon R \to {\mathbb{R}}$ a Riemann integrable function such that $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in R$. Show that if $\int_R f = 0$, then there is a measure zero set $E \subset R$ such that $f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in R \setminus E$ (one says “$f=0$ almost everywhere”). Note: This exercise in particular implies the rather subtle statement: If $f(x) > 0$ for all $x \in R$, then $\int_R f > 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.5 · Exercise 2
q: Prove that a bounded convex set is Jordan measurable. Hint: Induction on dimension.

title: Basic Analysis 10.5 · Exercise 4
q:
Let us construct an example of a non-Jordan measurable open set. Start in one dimension. Let $\{ r_j \}_{j=1}^\infty$ be an enumeration of all rational numbers in $(0,1)$. Let $(a_j,b_j)$ be open intervals such that $(a_j,b_j) \subset (0,1)$ for all $j$, $r_j \in (a_j,b_j)$, and $\sum_{j=1}^\infty (b_j-a_j) < {1}/{2}$. Now let $U := \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty (a_j,b_j)$.

(a) Show the open intervals $(a_j,b_j)$ as above actually exist.

(b) Prove $\partial U = [0,1] \setminus U$.

(c) Prove $\partial U$ is not of measure zero, and therefore $U$ is not Jordan measurable.

(d) Show that $W := \bigl( U \times (0,2) \bigr) \cup \bigl( (0,1) \times (1,2) \bigr)$ is a connected bounded open set in ${\mathbb{R}}^2$ that is not Jordan measurable.

title: Basic Analysis 10.5 · Exercise 5
q:
Suppose $K \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed measure zero set.

(a) If $K$ is bounded, prove that $K$ is Jordan measurable.

(b) If $S \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is bounded and Jordan measurable, prove that $S \setminus K$ is Jordan measurable.

(c) Construct a bounded Jordan measurable $S \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ and a bounded $T \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ of measure zero, such that neither $T$ nor $S \setminus T$ is Jordan measurable.

title: Basic Analysis 10.5 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open and $K \subset U$ is compact. Find a compact Jordan measurable set $S$ such that $S \subset U$ and $K \subset S^\circ$ ($K$ is in the interior of $S$).

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 1
q:
Prove that a disc $B(p,r) \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is a type III domain, and prove that the orientation given by the parametrization $\gamma(t) = \bigl(x_0+r\cos(t),y_0+r\sin(t)\bigr)$ where $p = (x_0,y_0)$ is the positive orientation of the boundary $\partial B(p,r)$.

Note: Feel free to use what you know about sine and cosine from calculus.

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 2
q: Prove that a convex bounded domain with piecewise smooth boundary is a type III domain.

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 3
q: Suppose $V \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is a bounded domain with piecewise smooth boundary of type III and suppose that $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is an open set such that $\overline{V} \subset U$. Suppose $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a twice continuously differentiable function. Prove that $\int_{\partial V} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \, dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \, dy = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 4
q:
For a disc $B(p,r) \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$, orient the boundary $\partial B(p,r)$ positively.

(a) Compute $\displaystyle \int_{\partial B(p,r)} -y \, dx$.

(b) Compute $\displaystyle \int_{\partial B(p,r)} x \, dy$.

(c) Compute $\displaystyle \int_{\partial B(p,r)} \frac{-y}{2} \, dx + \frac{x}{2} \, dy$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 6
q: Using the mean value property prove the maximum principle for harmonic functions: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^2$ is a connected open set and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is harmonic. Prove that if $f$ attains a maximum at $p \in U$, then $f$ is constant.

title: Basic Analysis 10.6 · Exercise 7
q:
Let $f(x,y) := \ln \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$.

(a) Show $f$ is harmonic where defined.

(b) Show $\lim\limits_{(x,y) \to 0} f(x,y) = -\infty$.

(c) Using a circle $C_r$ of radius $r$ around the origin, compute $\frac{1}{2\pi r} \int_{C_r} f \, ds$. What happens as $r \to 0$?

(d) Why can't you use Green's theorem in part c)?

title: Basic Analysis 10.7 · Exercise 2
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open and $S \subset U$ is a compact Jordan measurable set. Show that there exist finitely many closed rectangles $P_1,P_2, \ldots, P_k$ such that $P_j \subset U$, $S \subset P_1 \cup P_2 \cup \cdots \cup P_k$, and the interiors are mutually disjoint, that is, $P_j^\circ \cap P^\circ_\ell = \emptyset$ whenever $j \neq \ell$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.7 · Exercise 3
q:
Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is open, $x \in U$, and $g \colon U \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a continuously differentiable mapping. For every $c > 0$, show that

$$\bigl\{ y \in U : \bigl\lVert {g'(x)-g'(y)} \bigr\rVert < c \bigr\}$$

is an open set.

title: Basic Analysis 10.7 · Exercise 4
q: Suppose $R \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a closed rectangle. Show that if $\delta > 0$ is sufficiently small relative to the sides of $R$, then $R$ can be partitioned into subrectangles where each side $s$ of every subrectangle satisfies $\frac{\delta}{2} \leq s \leq \delta$.

title: Basic Analysis 10.7 · Exercise 5
q:
Prove the following version of the theorem: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a Riemann integrable compactly supported function. Suppose $K \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is the support of $f$, $S$ is a compact set, and $g \colon {\mathbb{R}}^n \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a function that when restricted to a neighborhood $U$ of $S$ is one-to-one and continuously differentiable, $g(S) = K$ and $J_g$ is never zero on $S$ (in the formula assume $J_g(x) = 0$ if $g$ is not differentiable at $x$, that is, when $x \notin U$). Then

$$\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^n} f\bigl(g(x)\bigr) \, \bigl\lvert {J_g(x)} \bigr\rvert \, dx = \int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}} f(u) \, du .$$

title: Basic Analysis 10.7 · Exercise 6
q:
Prove the following version of the theorem: Suppose $S \subset {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is an open bounded Jordan measurable set, $g \colon S \to {\mathbb{R}}^n$ is a one-to-one continuously differentiable mapping such that $J_g$ is never zero on $S$, and such that $g(S)$ is bounded and Jordan measurable (it is also open). Suppose $f \colon g(S) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is Riemann integrable. Then $f \circ g$ is Riemann integrable on $S$ and

$$\int_S f\bigl(g(x)\bigr) \, \bigl\lvert {J_g(x)} \bigr\rvert \, dx = \int_{g(S)} f(u) \, du .$$

Hint: Write $S$ as an increasing union of compact Jordan measurable sets, then apply the theorem of the section to those. Then prove that you can take the limit.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 1
q: Check that ${\mathbb{C}}$ is a field.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 2
q: Prove that for $z,w \in {\mathbb{C}}$, we have $\lvert {zw} \rvert = \lvert {z} \rvert \, \lvert {w} \rvert$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 6
q:
Given $x +iy$ define the matrix $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{smallmatrix} \right]$. Prove:

(a) The action of this matrix on a vector $(s,t)$ is the same as multiplying $(x+iy)(s+it)$.

(b) Multiplying two such matrices is the same multiplying the underlying complex numbers and then finding the corresponding matrix for the product. In other words, the field ${\mathbb{C}}$ can be identified with a subset of the 2-by-2 matrices.

(c) The matrix $\left[ \begin{smallmatrix} x & -y \\ y & x \end{smallmatrix} \right]$ has eigenvalues $x+iy$ and $x-iy$. Recall that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of a matrix $A$ if $A-\lambda I$ (a complex matrix in our case) is not invertible, that is, if it has linearly dependent rows: one row is a (complex) multiple of the other.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 7
q: Prove the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem for complex sequences. Suppose $\{ z_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a bounded sequence of complex numbers. That is, there exists an $M$ such that $\lvert {z_n} \rvert \leq M$ for all $n$. Prove that there exists a subsequence $\{ z_{n_k} \}_{k=1}^\infty$ that converges to some $z \in {\mathbb{C}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 8
q:
(a) Prove that there is no simple mean value theorem for complex-valued functions: Find a differentiable function $f \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{C}}$ such that $f(0) = f(1) = 0$, but $f'(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in [0,1]$.

(b) However, there is a weaker form of the mean value theorem as there is for vector-valued functions. Prove: If $f \colon [a,b] \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is continuous and differentiable in $(a,b)$, and for some $M$, $\bigl\lvert {f'(x)} \bigr\rvert \leq M$ for all $x \in (a,b)$, then $\bigl\lvert {f(b)-f(a)} \bigr\rvert \leq M \lvert {b-a} \rvert$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.1 · Exercise 9
q: Prove that there is no simple mean value theorem for integrals for complex-valued functions: Find a continuous function $f \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{C}}$ such that $\int_0^1 f = 0$ but $f(t) \neq 0$ for all $t \in [0,1]$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.2 · Exercise 3
q: Suppose $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space. Prove that the uniform norm $\lVert {\cdot} \rVert_X$ is a norm on the vector space of continuous complex-valued functions $C(X,{\mathbb{C}})$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.2 · Exercise 4
q:
(a) Prove that $f_n(x) := 2^{-n} \sin(2^n x)$ converge uniformly to zero, but there exists a dense set $D \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n'(x) = 1$ for all $x \in D$.

(b) Prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2^{-n} \sin(2^n x)$ converges uniformly to a continuous function, and there exists a dense set $D \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ where the derivatives of the partial sums do not converge.

title: Basic Analysis 11.2 · Exercise 5
q: Prove that $\lVert {f} \rVert_{C^1} := \lVert {f} \rVert_{[a,b]}+\lVert {f'} \rVert_{[a,b]}$ is a norm on the vector space of continuously differentiable complex-valued functions $C^1\bigl([a,b],{\mathbb{C}}\bigr)$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.2 · Exercise 9
q: Suppose $f_n \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ are monotone increasing functions and suppose that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n$ converges pointwise. Prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n$ converges uniformly.

title: Basic Analysis 11.2 · Exercise 10
q:
Prove that

$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty e^{-nx}$$

converges for all $x > 0$ to a differentiable function.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 1
q:
Let

$$a_{k,m} := \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k=m,\\ -2^{k-m} & \text{if } k<m,\\ 0 & \text{if } k>m. \end{cases}$$

Compute (or show the limit doesn't exist):

a) $\displaystyle \sum_{m=1}^\infty \lvert {a_{k,m}} \rvert~$ for all $k$,

b) $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^\infty \lvert {a_{k,m}} \rvert~$ for all $m$,

c) $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{m=1}^\infty \lvert {a_{k,m}} \rvert$,

d) $\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^\infty \sum_{m=1}^\infty a_{k,m}$,

e) $\displaystyle \sum_{m=1}^\infty \sum_{k=1}^\infty a_{k,m}$.

Hint: Fubini for sums does not apply. In fact, answers to d) and e) are different.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 2
q:
Let $f(x) := \frac{1}{1+x^2}$. Prove that

(a) $f$ is an analytic function on all of ${\mathbb{R}}$ by finding a power series for $f$ at every $a \in {\mathbb{R}}$,

(b) the radius of convergence of the power series for $f$ at the origin is 1.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 3
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{C}} \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic. Show that for each $n$, there are at most finitely many zeros of $f$ in $B(0,n)$, that is, $f^{-1}(0) \cap B(0,n)$ is finite for each $n$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 4
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ is open and connected, $0 \in U$, and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic. Treating $f$ as a function of a real $x$ at the origin, suppose $f^{(n)}(0) = 0$ for all $n$. Show that $f(z) = 0$ for all $z \in U$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 5
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ is open and connected, $0 \in U$, and $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic. For real $x$ and $y$, let $h(x) := f(x)$ and $g(y) := -i \, f(iy)$. Show that $h$ and $g$ are infinitely differentiable at the origin and $h'(0) = g'(0)$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 6
q: Suppose a function $f$ is analytic in some neighborhood of the origin, and that there exists an $M$ such that $\lvert {f^{(n)}(0)} \rvert \leq M$ for all $n$. Prove that the series of $f$ at the origin converges for all $z \in {\mathbb{C}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 7
q: Suppose $f(z) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n z^n$ with a radius of convergence 1. Suppose $f(0) = 0$, but $f$ is not the zero function. Show that there exists a $k \in {\mathbb{N}}$ and a convergent power series $g(z) := \sum_{n=0}^\infty d_n z^n$ with radius of convergence 1 such that $f(z) = z^k g(z)$ for all $z \in B(0,1)$, and $g(0) \neq 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 8
q: Suppose $U \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ is open and connected. Suppose that $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic, $U \cap {\mathbb{R}} \neq \emptyset$ and $f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in U \cap {\mathbb{R}}$. Show that $f(z) = 0$ for all $z \in U$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 9
q:
For $\alpha \in {\mathbb{C}}$ and $k=0,1,2,3\ldots$, define

$$\binom{\alpha}{k} := \frac{\alpha(\alpha-1)\cdots(\alpha-k+1)}{k!} .$$

(a) Show that the series

$$f(z) := \sum_{k=0}^\infty \binom{\alpha}{k} z^k$$

converges whenever $\lvert {z} \rvert < 1$. In fact, prove that for $\alpha = 0,1,2,3,\ldots$ the radius of convergence is $\infty$, and for all other $\alpha$ the radius of convergence is 1.

(b) Show that for $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$, $\lvert {x} \rvert < 1$, we have

$$(1+x) f'(x) = \alpha f(x) ,$$

meaning that $f(x) = (1+x)^\alpha$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 10
q: Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{C}} \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic and suppose that for some open interval $(a,b) \subset {\mathbb{R}}$, $f$ is real-valued on $(a,b)$. Show that $f$ is real-valued on ${\mathbb{R}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.3 · Exercise 11
q: Let ${\mathbb{D}} := B(0,1)$ be the unit disc. Suppose $f \colon {\mathbb{D}} \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic with power series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n z^n$. Suppose $\lvert {c_n} \rvert \leq 1$ for all $n$. Prove that for all $z \in {\mathbb{D}}$, we have $\bigl\lvert {f(z)} \bigr\rvert \leq \frac{1}{1-\lvert {z} \rvert}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 1
q: Derive the power series for $\sin(z)$ and $\cos(z)$ at the origin.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 2
q: Using the power series, show that for real $x$, we have $\frac{d}{dx} \bigl[ \sin(x)\bigr] = \cos(x)$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \bigl[ \cos(x)\bigr] = -\sin(x)$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 3
q: Finish the proof of the argument showing that $x \mapsto e^{ix}$ from $[0,2\pi)$ is onto the unit circle. In particular, assume that we get all points of the form $(a,b)$ where $a^2+b^2=1$ and $a \geq 0$. By multiplying by $e^{i\pi}$ or $e^{-i\pi}$, show that we get everything, that is, even points where $a < 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 4
q: Show that the exponential is onto ${\mathbb{C}} \setminus \{ 0 \}$, and in fact, that for every nonzero $w$, there are infinitely many $z \in {\mathbb{C}}$ such that $e^z=w$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 5
q: Prove that for every $w \neq 0$ and every $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a $z \in {\mathbb{C}}$ with $\lvert {z} \rvert < \epsilon$ such that $e^{1/z} = w$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 6
q: We showed ${\bigl( \cos(x) \bigr)}^2 + {\bigl( \sin(x) \bigr)}^2 = 1$ for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$. Prove that ${\bigl( \cos(z) \bigr)}^2 + {\bigl( \sin(z) \bigr)}^2 = 1$ for all $z \in {\mathbb{C}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 7
q: Prove the trigonometric identities $\sin(z + w) = \sin(z) \cos(w) + \cos(z) \sin(w)$ and $\cos(z + w) = \cos(z) \cos(w) - \sin(z) \sin(w)$ for all $z,w \in {\mathbb{C}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 8
q: Define $\operatorname{sinc}(z) := \frac{\sin(z)}{z}$ for $z \neq 0$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(0) := 1$. Show that sinc is analytic and compute its power series at zero.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 9
q: Derive the power series at the origin for the hyperbolic sine and cosine.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 10
q:
Show

(a) $\sinh(0) = 0$, $\cosh(0) = 1$.

(b) For $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$, $\frac{d}{dx} \bigl[ \sinh(x) \bigr] = \cosh(x)$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \bigl[ \cosh(x) \bigr] = \sinh(x)$.

(c) $\cosh(x) > 0$ for all $x \in {\mathbb{R}}$ and $\sinh(x)$ is strictly increasing and bijective from ${\mathbb{R}}$ to ${\mathbb{R}}$.

(d) ${\bigl(\cosh(x)\bigr)}^2 = 1 + {\bigl(\sinh(x)\bigr)}^2$ for all $x$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 11
q:
Define $\tan(x) := \frac{\sin(x)}{\cos(x)}$ as usual.

(a) Show that for $x \in ({-\pi}/{2},{\pi}/{2})$, both $\sin$ and $\tan$ are strictly increasing, and hence the inverses $\arcsin$ and $\arctan$ exist when we restrict to that interval.

(b) Show that $\arcsin$ and $\arctan$ are differentiable and that $\frac{d}{dx} \arcsin(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$ and $\frac{d}{dx} \arctan(x) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}$.

(c) Using the finite geometric sum formula, show

$$\arctan(x) = \int_0^x \frac{1}{1+t^2} dt = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{{(-1)}^k}{2k+1} x^{2k+1}$$

converges for all $-1 \leq x \leq 1$ (including the end points). Hint: Integrate the finite sum, not the series.

(d) Use this to show that

$$1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \cdots = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{{(-1)}^k}{2k+1} = \frac{\pi}{4} .$$

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 14
q: Let $U \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ be open and $z_0 \in U$. Suppose $f \colon U \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is analytic and $f(z_0) = 0$. Show that there exists an $\epsilon > 0$ such that either $f(z) \neq 0$ for all $z$ with $0 < \lvert {z} \rvert < \epsilon$ or $f(z) = 0$ for all $z \in B(z_0,\epsilon)$. In other words, zeros of analytic functions are isolated. Of course, same holds for polynomials.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 15
q:
Show that a rational function that is not identically zero has at most finitely many zeros and singularities. In fact, show that if $p$ is a polynomial of degree $n > 0$ it has at most $n$ zeros.

Hint: If $z_0$ is a zero of $p$, then without loss of generality assume $z_0 = 0$. Then use induction.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 16
q:
Prove that if $z_0$ is a removable singularity of a rational function $f(z) := \frac{p(z)}{q(z)}$, then there exist polynomials $\widetilde{p}$ and $\widetilde{q}$ such that $\widetilde{q}(z_0) \neq 0$ and $f(z) = \frac{\widetilde{p}(z)}{\widetilde{q}(z)}$.

Hint: Without loss of generality assume $z_0 = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.4 · Exercise 18
q:
Let $f$ be a rational function and $S \subset {\mathbb{C}}$ be the set of the singularities of $f$. Prove that $f$ is equal to a nonconstant polynomial on ${\mathbb{C}} \setminus S$ if and only if $f$ has a pole at infinity and all the singularities are removable.

Hint: See exercises above.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 1
q: Let $f_n \colon [-1,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ be given by $f_n(x) := \frac{nx}{1+{(nx)}^2}$. Prove that the sequence is uniformly bounded, converges pointwise to 0, yet there is no subsequence that converges uniformly. Which hypothesis of Arzel\`a–Ascoli is not satisfied? Prove your assertion.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 2
q: Define $f_n \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$ by $f_n(x) := \frac{1}{{(x-n)}^2+1}$. Prove that this sequence is uniformly bounded, uniformly equicontinuous, the sequence converges pointwise to zero, yet there is no subsequence that converges uniformly. Which hypothesis of Arzel\`a–Ascoli is not satisfied? Prove your assertion.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 3
q: Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space, $C > 0$, $0 < \alpha \leq 1$, and suppose $f_n \colon X \to {\mathbb{C}}$ are functions such that $\bigl\lvert {f_n(x)-f_n(y)} \bigr\rvert \leq C {d(x,y)}^\alpha$ for all $x,y \in X$ and $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$. Suppose also that there is a point $p \in X$ such that $f_n(p) = 0$ for all $n$. Show that there exists a uniformly convergent subsequence converging to an $f \colon X \to {\mathbb{C}}$ that also satisfies $f(p) = 0$ and $\bigl\lvert {f(x)-f(y)} \bigr\rvert \leq C {d(x,y)}^\alpha$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 7
q: Suppose $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space, $\{ f_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ a uniformly equicontinuous sequence of functions in $C(X,{\mathbb{C}})$. Suppose $\{ f_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges pointwise. Show that it converges uniformly.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 8
q: Suppose that $\{ f_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a uniformly equicontinuous uniformly bounded sequence of $2\pi$-periodic functions $f_n \colon {\mathbb{R}} \to {\mathbb{R}}$. Show that there is a uniformly convergent subsequence.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 9
q: Show that for a compact metric space $X$, a sequence $\{ f_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ that is equicontinuous at every $x \in X$ is uniformly equicontinuous.

title: Basic Analysis 11.5 · Exercise 11
q:
Prove the Peano existence theorem (note the weaker hypotheses than Picard, but also the lack of uniqueness in this theorem):

Theorem: Suppose $F \colon I \times J \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a continuous function where $I, J \subset {\mathbb{R}}$ are closed bounded intervals, let $I^\circ$ and $J^\circ$ be their interiors, and let $(x_0,y_0) \in I^\circ \times J^\circ$. Then there exists an $h > 0$ and a differentiable function $f \colon [x_0 - h, x_0 + h] \to J \subset {\mathbb{R}}$, such that

$$f'(x) = F\bigl(x,f(x)\bigr) \qquad \text{and} \qquad f(x_0) = y_0.$$

We can prove this theorem by applying Euler's method for numerical solutions to ODE and showing that there is a subsequence of these approximations that converges.

(a) Show that there exists an $h > 0$ so that the following functions $f_n$ and $s_n$ are well-defined on $[x_0,x_0+h]$ for all $n \in {\mathbb{N}}$. Define $f_n(x_0) := y_0$ and $s_n(x_0) := F(x_0,y_0)$ and for each $\ell=0,1,\ldots,n-1$ in turn for $x \in \bigl(x_0+\frac{h\ell}{n},x_0+\frac{h(\ell+1)}{n}\bigr]$ let $s_n(x) := F\bigl(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}, f_n(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n})\bigr)$ and

$$\begin{aligned} f_n(x) & := f_n\bigl(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}\bigr) + \bigl(x-x_0-\tfrac{h\ell}{n}\bigr) F\bigl(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}, f_n(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}) \bigr) \\ & = f_n\bigl(x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}\bigr) + \int_{x_0+\tfrac{h\ell}{n}}^x s_n(t) \, dt \\ & = y_0 + \int_{x_0}^x s_n(t) \, dt . \end{aligned}$$

(b) Show that $\{ f_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is equicontinuous (in fact, Lipschitz with the same constant) and uniformly bounded. Arzel\`a–Ascoli then says that there exists a uniformly convergent subsequence $\{ f_{n_k} \}_{k=1}^\infty$ converging to a continuous $f$ defined on $[x_0,x_0+h]$.

(c) Prove that for all $x \in [x_0,x_0+h]$,

$$\int_{x_0}^x s_{n_k}(t) \, dt \quad \text{converges to} \quad \int_{x_0}^x F\bigl(t,f(t)\bigr) \, dt ,$$

and therefore, by applying the fundamental theorem of calculus, $f$ is differentiable on $[x_0,x_0+h]$ and $f'(x) = F\bigl(x,f(x)\bigr)$. Hint 1: $F$ is uniformly continuous. Hint 2: Show that $s_{n_k}$ converges uniformly.

(d) Use the solution above to show that $f$ can be defined in $[x_0-h,x_0]$ as well, possibly for a smaller $h > 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 2
q: Suppose $X := {\mathbb{R}}$ (not compact in particular). Show that $f(t) := e^t$ is not possible to uniformly approximate by polynomials on $X$. Hint: Consider $\bigl\lvert {\frac{e^t}{t^n}} \bigr\rvert$ as $t \to \infty$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 3
q:
Suppose $f \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{C}}$ is a uniform limit of a sequence of polynomials of degree at most $d$. Show that the limit is a polynomial of degree at most $d$. Conclude that to approximate a function which is not a polynomial, we need the degree of the approximations to go to infinity.

Hint: First prove that if a sequence of polynomials of degree $d$ converges uniformly to the zero function, then the coefficients converge to zero. One way to do this is linear algebra: Consider a polynomial $p$ evaluated at $d+1$ points to be a linear operator taking the coefficients of $p$ to the values of $p$ (an operator in $L({\mathbb{R}}^{d+1})$).

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 4
q: Suppose $f \colon [0,1] \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is continuous and $\int_0^1 f(x) x^n \, dx = 0$ for all $n = 0,1,2,\ldots$. Show that $f(x) = 0$ for all $x \in [0,1]$. Hint: Approximate by polynomials to show that $\int_0^1 {\bigl( f(x) \bigr)}^2 \, dx = 0$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 5
q: Suppose $I \colon C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr) \to {\mathbb{R}}$ is a linear continuous function such that $I(x^n) = \frac{1}{n+1}$ for all $n=0,1,2,3,\ldots$. Prove that $I(f) = \int_0^1 f$ for all $f \in C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 6
q:
Let ${\mathscr{A}}$ be the collection of real polynomials in $x^2$, that is, polynomials of the form $c_0 + c_1 x^2 + c_2 x^4 + \cdots + c_d x^{2d}$.

(a) Show that every $f \in C\bigl([0,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$ is a uniform limit of polynomials from ${\mathscr{A}}$.

(b) Find an $f \in C\bigl([-1,1],{\mathbb{R}}\bigr)$ that is not a uniform limit of polynomials from ${\mathscr{A}}$.

(c) Which hypothesis of the real Stone–Weierstrass is not satisfied for the domain $[-1,1]$?

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 7
q:
Let $\lvert {z} \rvert=1$ define the unit circle $S^1 \subset {\mathbb{C}}$.

(a) Show that functions of the form

$$\sum_{k=-n}^n c_k\, z^k$$

are dense in $C(S^1,{\mathbb{C}})$. Notice the negative powers.

(b) Show that functions of the form

$$c_0 + \sum_{k=1}^n c_k \, z^k + \sum_{k=1}^n c_{-k}\, \bar{z}^k$$

are dense in $C(S^1,{\mathbb{C}})$. These functions are called harmonic polynomials, and this approximation leads to, for example, the solution of the steady state heat problem.

Hint: A good way to write the equation for $S^1$ is $z \bar{z} = 1$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 8
q:
Show that any continuous function $f \colon [-\pi,\pi] \to {\mathbb{C}}$ with $f(-\pi)=f(\pi)$ can be approximated uniformly by functions of the form

$$\sum_{k=-n}^n c_k \, e^{ik x}$$

for complex numbers $c_k$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 10
q: Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space and suppose ${\mathscr{A}} \subset C(X,{\mathbb{R}})$ is a real algebra that separates points, but vanishes at exactly one point $x_0 \in X$. That is, $f(x_0) = 0$ for all $f \in {\mathscr{A}}$, but for every $y \in X \setminus \{ x_0 \}$ there is a $\varphi \in {\mathscr{A}}$ such that $\varphi(y) \neq 0$. Prove that every function $g \in C(X,{\mathbb{R}})$ such that $g(x_0) = 0$ is a uniform limit of functions from ${\mathscr{A}}$.

title: Basic Analysis 11.6 · Exercise 11
